title: Sound before meaning
hookLine: Japji is meant to be heard; we will listen to each pauri before we learn what it says
last: GURMUKHI — READ WITH THE MOUTH FIRST.

lines: JAPJI AT DAWN, FROM THE KITCHEN.
cards: A lullaby in a language you don't speak can still get through. So can a chant in a stadium, or a hymn at a wedding where you catch one word in ten. The meaning never arrives.

The sound does, and it stays. Japji often reaches people that way first. In homes where it's recited at dawn, children hear it drifting from a kitchen or a car radio long before anyone explains what it says.

teach.b: So this camp has a rule. Almost every pauri, every stanza, gets two days. Day one is sound: listen, and say the opening line out loud.
Day two is meaning: what the Guru is saying. Why that order? Partly because of what Japji is.
The name comes from jap, to recite, to repeat.

teach.h: JAPJI IS MADE TO BE SAID.
teach.b: It was made to be said, not only studied.
It's the first bani of the morning Nitnem, often said from memory: thirty-eight pauris, with a short salok at the start and another at the end, and a steady recitation fits into an ordinary morning.
Partly because of how Gurbani, the Guru's word, speaks about itself.

teach.h: THE SHABAD WORKS ON THE LISTENER.
teach.b: The hymns keep praising the shabad, the word as sound, and the naad, the sound that moves through everything, as things that work on the one who hears them.
Japji itself will give four whole pauris to one word: suniai, by listening. And partly it's simply how learning works. Understanding goes deeper when it lands on something familiar.
If you've said a line thirty times, then on the day its meaning arrives, it has somewhere to sit. There's a humility in it, too.

You don't have to understand everything before you start. And if you grew up Sikh and can't read Gurmukhi, or follow only some of the Punjabi in the hymns, you're in large company, especially far from Punjab.
Some people carry a quiet embarrassment about that.
There's no need. The Granth's language is centuries old, fluent speakers look words up too, and this camp is built for exactly where you are.
When the meanings open, i'll follow Macauliffe's 1909 translation, retold in plain words. For now, the instruction is short. Listen.

how: Sikhs recite or listen to Japji Sahib each morning, often from memory, as the first bani of Nitnem; children often hear it long before they study its meaning.

games.q: you're about to start learning Japji. what does this camp ask you to do first?
o: study a translation of the whole thing.
listen to it, and say the opening line aloud.
games.why: sound first, meaning second: each pauri is heard and said before it is explained.

practice: Close your eyes and listen to whatever is around you, the hum of a fridge, traffic, a bird, your own breath, without naming the sounds.
If you have a recording of Japji Sahib, and there are many, let it play and wash past you, without following the words or looking anything up. If you pray, simply sit inside it.

wordCard.voice: Japji Sahib. In this camp, each pauri of it is heard and said before it is explained, sound before meaning.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak's morning hymn; ji and sahib add respect.

carryVoice: Your line: listen before you understand. The meaning can wait its turn. That's day one hundred fifty-eight.
